content.title: About
content.content: A doughnut is a small sweet fried or baked pastry, often topped with chocolate icing. The batter is usually made from wheat flour, eggs, milk, sugar and yeast, and after cooking it is coated with a smooth chocolate glaze, sometimes sprinkled with nuts or sprinkles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Doughnuts originated in Europe in the 19th century and quickly became popular in the United States.
The classic American doughnut has a ring shape, while in Russia and many other countries doughnuts are often without a hole.
Chocolate icing may contain cocoa butter, powdered sugar and butter, giving it a glossy and creamy texture.
In some countries doughnuts are filled with jam, custard, cream or fruit puree.
Doughnuts are often associated with holidays – for example, they are a traditional treat on Thanksgiving in the US.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Doughnuts provide fast‑acting carbohydrates and sugar, making them a convenient quick snack.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: When made with whole‑grain flour, doughnuts can contain modest amounts of iron, which supports blood formation.

items.title: Calcium from dairy
items.content: Milk and butter in the batter supply calcium, essential for bone health.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Trans and saturated fats
items.content: Frying in oil can add trans‑fats and saturated fats, which are unfavorable for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional doughnut batter contains wheat flour, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy doughnuts in moderation as a dessert or quick snack. They pair well with coffee, tea or milk. For extra indulgence, split them and add whipped cream or fruit sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store doughnuts in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator, where they stay fresh for about a week but may become less soft.
